audience.programmeDescription: This primarily Dutch-taught bachelor studies how religion, culture and political power shape one another, with particular attention to Europe and the Middle East.
audience.comparisonExplanation: This comparison assesses the documented 67.5 EC political, cultural and religious subject and method core. UCR can combine political authority and rights, social theory, media and cultural interpretation, global history, myth, religious art and concrete research methods in broader programmes. Systematic Abrahamic history, Bible/Quran exegesis, Muhammad studies and dedicated religious-prejudice history remain differences. The specialisation, final research, unidentified 7.5 EC course and complete degree progression are excluded. The 60 EC profiling space is shown without assumed contents.

curriculum.limitation: The outline documents 172.5 of 180 EC. Only the nine named subject and method courses (67.5 EC) are assessed. The 30 EC specialisation and 15 EC final research are retained but unassessed; the other required 7.5 EC is unidentified. The 60 EC profiling space has no selected contents. Full cohort progression and degree equivalence are not certified.

componentNotes.pcr-pc1v26001: Introduces how political power, cultural practices and religious authority interact, using theory and historical and current cases.
componentNotes.pcr-pc1v26002: Studies Judaism, Christianity and Islam as changing traditions shaped through historical interaction.
componentNotes.pcr-pc2v26001: Studies the contexts, interpretation and political and cultural uses of the Bible and Quran, including a text-research project.
componentNotes.pcr-pc1v26003: Analyses authority, identity and exclusion in new media and popular culture.
componentNotes.pcr-pc2v26002: Introduces anthropological theory and methods through observation, interviews and a small ethnographic study in a religious setting.
componentNotes.pcr-pc2v26003: Studies legitimacy, sovereignty and political power through historical political texts from different traditions.
componentNotes.pcr-pc2v26004: Analyses conspiracy theories through historical, social-scientific and religious-studies perspectives.
componentNotes.pcr-pc2v26005: Studies antisemitism and Islamophobia through history, theory, discourse and visual analysis.
componentNotes.pcr-ia2v17001: Studies historical and later representations of Muhammad in Islamic traditions and Western culture. Knowledge of Islam is expected; Tradition in Change provides preparation.
componentNotes.pcr-depth-politics-religion: This is a confirmed 30 EC specialisation requirement. Its four-course content and entry rules for the 2026 intake remain unconfirmed. This component is retained but outside the assessed 67.5 EC core.
componentNotes.pcr-thesis-preparation: A required 7.5 EC research seminar prepares the final project. Current programme guidance places it in block 3 before the thesis. This component is retained but outside the assessed 67.5 EC core.
componentNotes.pcr-thesis: A required 7.5 EC thesis follows the research seminar, with supervision and assessment by two teachers. The current programme guidance places it in block 4. This component is retained but outside the assessed 67.5 EC core.
componentNotes.pcr-profile: A coherent 30 EC package may be a minor, study abroad or a second specialisation. Non-Utrecht minors and foreign study require prior examination-board approval.
componentNotes.pcr-open: Another 30 EC is open study. Across the full 60 EC profiling space, at least 15 EC must be at intermediate or advanced level. Internships can contribute up to 15 EC; master’s courses are excluded. Overlapping content may lead to a proportional credit reduction.

trace: Political authority and rights support questions of sovereignty and legitimacy.
Social structure, belonging and othering support analysis of cultural boundaries.
Media analysis supports study of cultural representation across media.
Interviews, observation, documentary sources and reflexivity support study of lived practice.
Divine command, relativism, duties and care support normative study.
International relations theories support analysis of conflict across borders.
Empirical design, measurement, sampling, original data collection and statistical analysis provide methodological support for studying beliefs or identities; no guaranteed religious dataset.
Social construction, stigma and intersectionality support study of prejudice.
Rights law and its foundations support analysis of pluralism and protections.
Legal systems, justice, social control, race/gender and socio-legal research supply legal and normative tools for authority and pluralism.

Comparative Greek/Roman/NearEastern/Indian/Arabic/African myth and narrative transmission directly examine creation, divine succession, cultural power, gender and meaning through primary-source research. This positive religion-related content broadens earlier research.
Structural violence, historical grievances and peacebuilding support conflict inquiry.
Comparative constitutional rights, state institutions, administrative participation and remedies support public-power and religious-freedom analysis; no full theology or comparative religious law.

Indigenous history, boarding schools, institutional violence, traditional knowledge and cultural resurgence supply concrete study of colonial power, identity and cultural resistance beyond the previous narrow palette.

Official description provides actual religious/cross-cultural art connections through Islamic courts, Mediterranean trade, colonisation and Renaissance production. Fullconsiderationofdescription-onlycourse; no invented fieldwork or assessment.
Civil society, publics, migrant solidarity and hegemony support analysis of institutions and identity.
Representation, exclusion and racial extremism support study of media and power.
Radicalization, identity and resilience support psychosocial study of extremism.
Primary texts and archaeological evidence examine Athenian political authority, myth, ritual and civic identity. Direct religion-politics-cultural-expression anchor, not merely democracy adjacency.
Documentary representation, propaganda, ethnography, ethics and interviewing/production support inquiry into lived identities and cultural authority without promising a religious documentary topic.
Actual Greek/Indian emotion traditions, fear, grief and political anger connect meaning, affect and public life; not religion-specific experiential training.
Actual Buddhist non-self, identity and transformative experience strengthen reflection on self and belief. Not comparative mysticism or a religious experience field sequence.
Historical research design and source criticism support independent inquiry.
Knowledge, ethics and arguments about God support basic philosophical inquiry.
Close reading of narrative, symbols and voice supports interpretation of texts.
Artefact-based investigation of status, religion, gender and ancient social identities provides direct material-culture methods; not Abrahamic textual exegesis.
Historical religious/political context and close visual analysis of late-medieval/Renaissance and later paintings provide concrete material-cultural interpretation.
Western African art, religious/social authority, colonial collections and restitution supply a direct religion-culture-power relationship with independent art-historical research.

Historical media and digital storytelling analyse representation, conformity, Indigenous voice and disability-centred futures. Concrete mediapower complement; not presumedTikTokreligiousidentityspecialisation.
Actual intertextuality, adaptation, heritage and text-film research strengthen transmission/representation inquiry; no scriptural canon guaranteed.
Actual Greek/Indian agency, fate and moral responsibility deepen questions of freedom and selfhood, without treating all Indian philosophy as religion.
Actual feminist/Marxist/minority/psychoanalytic interpretation and independent textual research support situated cultural meaning; description-only, no added exegesis method.
Imperialism, migration and political ideologies ground modern diversity and conflict.
Imperial institutions and legitimacy support historical study of states and transnational rule.
Comparative institutions and nationalism support political contextualization.

alternatives.label: Public power, diversity and belief
alternatives.concept: Study how authority, law, social belonging and cultural representation shape public life. Political philosophy, human rights and constitutional comparison are combined with social theory, media and racialisation, radicalisation prevention and peacebuilding. World myth, ancient civic religion and Mediterranean cultural exchange provide concrete belief-related study, while qualitative, historical and empirical research supports independent inquiry. This is a broader response to the confirmed political-cultural-religious core; it does not reproduce Abrahamic history, scriptural exegesis or Muhammad studies.
alternatives.labelReason: Describes actual sustained study and distinct curricular priorities, without claiming a named UCR track, religiousstudies degree, regional specialization or full external equivalence.
progression: Foundation theory/methods in year1; comparative/criticalsubjectstudy in year2; advanced civic/social/media/interpretive research in year3. Actual GOSGATE102 precedes GOSLAWJ213. PPDyear1 inallthree. No invented prerequisites, no fourthcoursepadding.

alternatives.label: Myth, media and cultural meaning
alternatives.concept: Study how narratives, visual and material culture, media and philosophical ideas create meaning and shape authority. Comparative world myth, Western and African religious art, Mediterranean exchange and ancient civic religion anchor a cultural inquiry developed through film, documentary, literary interpretation and critical media research. Philosophical study of God, ethics, self and agency complements it. No continuous comparative mysticism, Abrahamic traditions, Bible/Quran commentary or specialist religious education is promised.

alternatives.label: Empires, cultural encounters and conflict
alternatives.concept: Study how empires, colonialism, states and cultural encounters shape identities, conflict and social boundaries. Modern and imperial history, Indigenous histories, international/comparative politics and peacebuilding combine with social theory, racialised media and tangible myth/religion/material-culture cases. Qualitative, statistical, documentary and historical research develop comparative inquiry. This offers a global historical response, without claiming sustained Middle Eastern history, Arabic or the excluded Utrecht specialisation.

notes.text: Only the documented 67.5 EC political, cultural and religious subject/method core is assessed. UCR offers broader programmes with genuine belief-related teaching, but systematic Abrahamic history, Bible/Quran exegesis, Muhammad studies and dedicated antisemitism/Islamophobia history remain differences. Specialisation, final research, the unidentified 7.5 EC requirement and complete external progression are excluded. The 60 EC profiling space has no assumed contents. Optional independent UCR research is additional to its scheduled 180 EC.

blocks: Both teach sovereignty, legitimacy and authority through historical political texts and comparative argument. This is a specific political-thought relationship; the Eastern/Western corpus and prophecy emphasis differ.

Both substantively analyze media meaning, power and representation, including digital platforms. UCR adds film form and critical feminist/postcolonial analysis; it does not reproduce Utrecht’s attention/experience economy or religious platform cases.

Both teach ethical and reflexive participant observation, interviews and original qualitative research. UCR provides these actual methods and analysis; it does not guarantee religious fieldwork or Utrecht’s lived-religion theory sequence.

The integrated politics, culture and religion framework remains distinct. UCR theory, ancient civic religion and religious art supply actual contributions, without a directly equivalent introductory module.
World myth, religious art and philosophy provide meaningful comparative study, but do not reproduce the systematic study of interacting Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
UCR literary and myth methods do not replace Bible and Quran academic editions, commentary, exegesis and the specified scriptural research.
Radicalisation prevention, misinformation, media and social theory contribute, without a dedicated historical and religious conspiracy course or social epistemology sequence.
Race, media, stigma and othering are substantial related study, but do not reproduce dedicated global antisemitism and Islamophobia history or its religious sources.
Muhammad’s historical sources, Islamic theological, legal and mystical constructions, and Western reception are not reproduced by global history or general religious culture.
The confirmed 30 EC requirement is retained. Its membership and progression are pending and outside the assessed core; no contents or UCR relationship are assumed.
The required 7.5 EC research preparation is retained outside the assessed core. Complete eligibility and equivalent culminating training are not certified.

The required 7.5 EC thesis is retained outside the assessed core. Future cohort progression and specialist research are unverified. Optional UCR research is additional, without an equivalent thesis claim.
The coherent 30 EC profiling category has no selected contents and is outside the academic claim. Approval, availability and nonoverlap conditions apply.
The 30 EC open category has no selected contents and is outside the academic claim; no particular course relationship is assumed.

acceptance.claim: Three complete feasible UCR programmes meaningfully respond to the confirmed 67.5 EC political-cultural-religious core through sustained authority/rights/social theory, cultural/media interpretation, comparative historical encounters, specific myth/art/civic-religion teaching and actual empirical/textual inquiry. Systematic Abrahamic history, scriptural exegesis, Muhammad study and dedicated religious-prejudice history remain substantive differences. The claim does not compare the specialisation, final research, missing required course, uninstantiated profiling or complete degree/progression.
